{{Short description|Line joining midpoints of a complete quadrilateral's 3 diagonals}}
[[File:Newton-Gauss Line Default Figure.svg|thumb|
{{legend-line|solid red|[[Diagonal]]s}}
{{legend-line|solid lime|'''Newton-Gauss line''' through the midpoints {{mvar|L, M, N}} of the diagonals}}]]

In [[geometry]], the '''Newton–Gauss line''' (or '''Gauss–Newton line''') is the [[Line (geometry)|line]] joining the [[midpoint]]s of the three [[diagonal]]s of a [[complete quadrilateral]].

The midpoints of the two diagonals of a [[Convex set|convex]] [[quadrilateral]] with at most two parallel sides are distinct and thus determine a line, the [[Newton line]]. If the sides of such a quadrilateral are extended to form a complete quadrangle, the diagonals of the quadrilateral remain diagonals of the complete quadrangle and the Newton line of the quadrilateral is the Newton–Gauss line of the complete quadrangle.
<!-- Hold until article is revised
The Newton–Gauss line is very similar to the [[Newton line]], which follows the same general [[theorem]] but uses a convex [[quadrilateral]] with at most two parallel sides; this also means instead of having three [[diagonal]]s, it uses the [[midpoint]] of the two [[diagonal]]s in addition to the point which [[Bisection|bisects]] two lines created by connecting the [[midpoint]]s of the opposite sides of the [[quadrilateral]].
-->

== Complete quadrilaterals ==
{{main|Complete quadrilateral}}

Any four lines in [[general position]] (no two lines are parallel, and no three are concurrent) form a [[complete quadrilateral]]. This [[Configuration (geometry)|configuration]] consists of a total of six points, the intersection points of the four lines, with three points on each line and precisely two lines through each point.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266061112|title=Gauss–Newton Lines and Eleven Point Conics|last=Alperin|first=Roger C.|author-link=Roger C. Alperin|date=6 January 2012|website=Research Gate}}</ref> These six points can be split into pairs so that the [[line segment]]s determined by any pair do not intersect any of the given four lines except at the endpoints. These three line segments are called [[diagonal]]s of the complete quadrilateral.

===Existence of the Newton−Gauss line===
[[File:Labeling for a complete quadrilateral.svg|right|350px|Labels used in proof concerning complete quadrilateral]]
It is a well-known theorem that the three midpoints of the diagonals of a complete quadrilateral are [[collinear]].<ref name=Johson62>{{harvnb|Johnson|2007|loc=p. 62}}</ref>
There are several proofs of the result based on areas <ref name=Johson62 /> or wedge products<ref>{{citation|first=Dan|last=Pedoe|title=Geometry A Comprehensive Course|year=1988|orig-year=1970|publisher=Dover|pages=46–47|isbn=0-486-65812-0}}</ref> or, as the following proof, on [[Menelaus's theorem]], due to Hillyer and published in 1920.<ref>{{harvnb|Johnson|2007|loc=p. 152}}</ref>

Let the complete quadrilateral {{mvar|ABCA'B'C'}} be labeled as in the diagram with diagonals {{mvar|{{overline|AA'}}, {{overline|BB'}}, {{overline|CC'}}}} and their respective midpoints {{mvar|L, M, N}}. Let the midpoints of {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}, {{overline|CA'}}, {{overline|A'B}}}} be {{mvar|P, Q, R}} respectively. Using similar triangles it is seen that {{mvar|QR}} intersects {{mvar|{{overline|AA'}}}} at {{mvar|L}}, {{mvar|RP}} intersects {{mvar|{{overline|BB'}}}} at {{mvar|M}} and {{mvar|PQ}} intersects {{mvar|{{overline|CC'}}}} at {{mvar|N}}. Again, similar triangles provide the following proportions,
<math display="block">\frac{\overline{RL}}{\overline{LQ}} = \frac{\overline{BA}}{\overline{AC}}, \quad \frac{\overline{QN}}{\overline{NP}} = \frac{\overline{A'C'}}{\overline{C'B}}, \quad \frac{\overline{PM}}{\overline{MR}} = \frac{\overline{CB'}}{\overline{B'A'}}.
</math>
However, the line {{math|''A'B'C ''}} intersects the sides of triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}, so by Menelaus's theorem the product of the terms on the right hand sides is −1. Thus, the product of the terms on the left hand sides is also −1 and again by Menelaus's theorem, the points {{mvar|L, M, N}} are collinear on the sides of triangle {{math|△''PQR''}}.

== Applications to cyclic quadrilaterals==

The following are some results that use the Newton–Gauss line of complete quadrilaterals that are associated with [[cyclic quadrilateral]]s, based on the work of Barbu and Patrascu.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2012volume12/FG201212.pdf|title=Some Properties of the Newton–Gauss Line|last=Patrascu|first=Ion|date=|website=Forum Geometricorum|access-date=29 April 2019|archive-date=29 March 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329151523/https://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2012volume12/FG201212.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Equal angles ===
[[File:Newton-Gauss_Line_Figure_1_subtext.png|thumb|''Figure 1:'' An angle equality.]]

Given any cyclic quadrilateral {{mvar|ABCD}}, let point {{mvar|F}} be the [[Line–line intersection|point of intersection]] between the two diagonals {{mvar|{{overline|AC}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|BD}}}}. Extend the diagonals {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}} until they meet at the point of intersection, {{mvar|E}}. Let the [[midpoint]] of the [[Line segment|segment]] {{mvar|{{overline|EF}}}} be {{mvar|N}}, and let the midpoint of the segment {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} be {{mvar|M}} (Figure 1).

==== Theorem ====
If the midpoint of the line segment {{mvar|{{overline|BF}}}} is {{mvar|P}}, the Newton–Gauss line of the complete quadrilateral {{mvar|ABCDEF}} and the line {{mvar|PM}} determine an angle {{math|∠''PMN''}} equal to {{math|∠''EFD''}}.

===== Proof =====
First show that the [[triangle]]s {{math|△''NPM'', △''EDF''}} are [[Similarity (geometry)|similar]].

Since {{math|''BE'' ∥ ''PN''}} and {{math|''FC'' ∥ ''PM''}}, we know {{math|1=∠''NPM'' = ∠''EAC''}}. Also, <math>\tfrac{\overline{BE}}{\overline{PN}} = \tfrac{\overline{FC}}{\overline{PM}} = 2.</math>

In the cyclic quadrilateral {{mvar|ABCD}}, these [[Equality (mathematics)|equalities]] hold:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\angle EDF &= \angle ADF + \angle EDA, \\
           &= \angle ACB + \angle ABC, \\
           &= \angle EAC.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, {{math|1=∠''NPM'' = ∠''EDF''}}.

Let {{math|''R''{{sub|1}}, ''R''{{sub|2}}}} be the [[Radius|radii]] of the [[Circumscribed circle|circumcircles]] of {{math|△''EDB'', △''FCD''}} respectively. Apply the [[law of sines]] to the triangles, to obtain:

<math display="block">\frac {\overline{BE}}{\overline{FC}}=\frac {2R_1\sin \angle EDB}{2R_2\sin \angle FDC}=\frac {R_1}{R_2}=\frac {2R_1\sin \angle EBD}{2R_2\sin \angle FCD} = \frac{\overline{DE}}{\overline{DF}}.</math>

Since {{math|1={{overline|''BE''}} = 2 · {{overline|''PN''}}}} and {{math|1={{overline|''FC''}} = 2 · {{overline|''PM''}}}}, this shows the equality <math>\tfrac{\overline{PN}}{\overline{PM}} = \tfrac{\overline{DE}}{\overline{DF}}.</math> The similarity of triangles {{math|△''PMN'', △''DFE''}} follows, and {{math|1=∠''NMP'' = ∠''EFD''}}.

===== Remark =====
If {{mvar|Q}} is the midpoint of the line segment {{mvar|{{overline|FC}}}}, it follows by the same reasoning that {{math|1=∠''NMQ'' = ∠''EFA''}}.
[[File:Newton-Gauss_Line_Figure_2_Subtext.png|thumb|''Figure 2:'' Isogonal lines.]]

=== Isogonal lines ===
==== Theorem ====
The line through {{mvar|E}} [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]] to the Newton–Gauss line of the complete quadrilateral {{mvar|ABCDEF}} and the line {{mvar|EF}} are isogonal lines of {{math|∠''BEC''}}, that is, each line is a [[Reflection (mathematics)|reflection]] of the other about the [[angle bisector]].<ref name=":2" /> (Figure 2)

===== Proof =====
Triangles  {{math|△''EDF'', △''NPM''}} are similar by the above argument, so {{math|1=∠''DEF'' = ∠''PNM''}}. Let {{mvar|E'}} be the point of intersection of {{mvar|BC}} and the line parallel to the Newton–Gauss line {{mvar|NM}} through {{mvar|E}}.

Since {{math|''PN'' ∥ ''BE''}} and {{math|''NM'' ∥ ''EE',''}} {{math|1=∠''BEF'' = ∠''PNF''}}, and {{math|1=∠''FNM'' = ∠''E'EF''}}.

Therefore, 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\angle CEE' &= \angle DEF - \angle E'EF, \\
            &= \angle PNM - \angle FNM, \\
            &= \angle PNF = \angle BEF.
\end{align}</math>

=== Two cyclic quadrilaterals sharing a Newton-Gauss line===

[[File:Newton-Gauss_Line_Subtext_3.1.png|thumb|''Figure 3:'' Showing that the quadrilaterals {{mvar|MPGN, MQHN}} are cyclic.]]

==== Lemma ====
Let {{mvar|G}} and {{mvar|H}} be the [[Projection (linear algebra)|orthogonal projections]] of the point {{mvar|F}} on the lines {{mvar|AB}} and {{mvar|CD}} respectively.

The [[quadrilateral]]s {{mvar|MPGN}} and  {{mvar|MQHN}} are cyclic quadrilaterals.<ref name=":2" />

===== Proof =====
{{math|1=∠''EFD'' = ∠''PMN''}}, as previously shown. The points {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|N}} are the respective [[Circumscribed circle|circumcenters]] of the [[right triangle]]s {{math|△''BFG'', △''EFG''}}. Thus, {{math|1=∠''PGF'' = ∠''PFG''}} and {{math|1=∠''FGN'' = ∠''GFN''}}.

Therefore,

<math display="block">\begin{align} 
\angle PGN + \angle PMN 
& = (\angle PGF + \angle FGN) + \angle PMN  \\[4pt] 
& = \angle PFG + \angle GFN + \angle EFD \\[4pt] 
&= 180^\circ 
\end{align}.</math>

Therefore, {{mvar|MPGN}} is a cyclic quadrilateral, and by the same reasoning, {{mvar|MQHN}} also lies on a circle.

[[File:Newton-Gauss_Line_Figure_3_subtext_2.png|thumb|''Figure 4:'' Showing that the complete quadrilaterals {{mvar|EDGHIJ, ABCDEF}} have the same Newton–Gauss line.]]

==== Theorem ====
Extend the lines {{mvar|GF, HF}} to intersect {{mvar|EC, EB}} at {{mvar|I, J}} respectively (Figure 4).

The complete quadrilaterals {{mvar|EFGHIJ}} and {{mvar|ABCDEF}} have the same Newton–Gauss line.<ref name=":2" />

===== Proof =====
The two complete quadrilaterals have a shared diagonal, {{mvar|{{overline|EF}}}}. {{mvar|N}} lies on the Newton–Gauss line of both quadrilaterals. {{mvar|N}} is [[equidistant]] from {{mvar|G}} and {{mvar|H}}, since it is the [[Circumscribed circle|circumcenter]] of the cyclic quadrilateral {{mvar|EGFH}}.

If triangles {{math|△''GMP'', △''HMQ''}} are [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]], and it will follow that {{mvar|M}} lies on the [[perpendicular bisector]] of the line {{mvar|HG}}. Therefore, the line {{mvar|MN}} contains the midpoint of {{mvar|{{overline|GH}}}}, and is the Newton–Gauss line of {{mvar|EFGHIJ}}.

To show that the triangles {{math|△''GMP'', △''HMQ''}} are congruent, first observe that {{mvar|PMQF}} is a [[parallelogram]], since the points {{mvar|M, P}} are midpoints of {{mvar|{{overline|BF}}, {{overline|BC}}}} respectively.

Therefore,

<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \overline{MP} = \overline{QF} = \overline{HQ}, \\
& \overline{GP} = \overline{PF} = \overline{MQ}, \\
& \angle MPF = \angle FQM.
\end{align}</math>

Also note that

<math display="block">\angle FPG = 2 \angle PBG = 2 \angle DBA = 2 \angle DCA = 2 \angle HCF = \angle HQF.</math>

Hence,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\angle MPG &= \angle MPF + \angle FPG, \\
           &= \angle FQM + \angle HQF, \\
           &= \angle HQF + \angle FQM, \\
           &= \angle HQM.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, {{math|△''GMP''}} and {{math|△''HMQ''}} are congruent by SAS.

===== Remark =====
Due to {{math|△''GMP'', △''HMQ''}} being congruent triangles, their [[Circumscribed circle|circumcircles]] {{mvar|MPGN, MQHN}} are also [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]].

== Relation with the Miquel point ==

The [[point at infinity]] along the Newton–Gauss line is the [[isogonal conjugate]] of the Miquel point.

==Generalization ==
Dao Thanh Oai showed a generalization of the Newton–Gauss line.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Generalizations of some famous classical Euclidean geometry theorems |journal=International Journal of Computer Discovered Mathematics  |last=Thanh Oai |first=Dao |url=https://journal-1.eu/2016-3/Dao-Thanh-Oai-Generalizations-pp.12-20.pdf |volume=3}}</ref>

For a triangle {{Mvar|ABC}}, let {{Mvar|l}} an arbitrary line and {{Math|''A''{{sub|0}}''B''{{sub|0}}''C''{{sub|0}}}} the [[Cevian triangle]] of an arbitrary point {{Mvar|P}}. {{Mvar|l}} intersects  {{Mvar|BC, CA}}, and {{Mvar|AB}} at {{Math|''A''{{sub|1}}, ''B''{{sub|1}},}} and {{Math|''C''{{sub|1}}}} respectively. Then {{Math|''AA''{{sub|1}}∩''B''{{sub|0}}''C''{{sub|0}}, ''BB''{{sub|1}}∩''C''{{sub|0}}''A''{{sub|0}}}}, and {{Math|''CC''{{sub|1}}∩''A''{{sub|0}}''B''{{sub|0}}}} are [[colinear]].

If {{Mvar|P}} is the [[centroid]] of the triangle {{Mvar|ABC}}, the line is Newton–Gauss line of the quadrilateral composed of {{Mvar|AB, BC, CA,}} and {{Mvar|l}}.

== History ==
The Newton–Gauss line proof was developed by the two mathematicians it is named after: [[Isaac Newton|Sir Isaac Newton]] and [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]].{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} The initial framework for this theorem is from the work of Newton, in his previous theorem on the [[Newton line]], in which Newton showed that the center of a conic inscribed in a quadrilateral lies on the Newton–Gauss line.<ref>{{citation|first=David|last=Wells|title=The Penguin Dictionary of Curious and Interesting Geometry|year=1991|publisher=Penguin Books|page=[https://archive.org/details/penguindictionar0000well/page/36 36]|isbn=978-0-14-011813-1|url=https://archive.org/details/penguindictionar0000well/page/36}}</ref>

The theorem of Gauss and Bodenmiller states that the three circles whose diameters are the diagonals of a complete quadrilateral are [[Coaxal circles|coaxal]].<ref>{{harvnb|Johnson|2007|loc=p. 172}}</ref>
